data.title: Appeal Court sentences Anon Nampa to prison for criticizing royal defamation law
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Appeal Court sentences Anon Nampa to prison for criticizing royal defamation law
The Appeal Court on 12 November sentenced human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to 4 years in prison on royal defamation and computer crimes charges for 3 Facebook posts which called for monarchy reform and criticized the use of the royal defamation law against critics of the monarchy.
Two of the posts, made on 1 January 2021, say that the royal defamation law should not be used to silence critics of the monarchy and that people should be able to talk about the monarchy when it comes to public matters even if they do not praise it. One of the posts also asks how losing faith in the monarchy could be an offense and if people are required to believe in the monarchy even if its members do not behave appropriately.
The third post, on 3 January 2021, criticized royalist groups for trying to silence dissidents when questions are raised about the monarchy. Anon wrote that royalists are refusing to see the problem when the problem is caused by the monarchy , such as lavish spending of the government’s money. He also asked if people would find it acceptable if the Prime Minister or other government official relocated to Germany and flew back and forth between Thailand and Germany with an entourage.
The complaint against Anon was filed by Nangnoi Assawakittikorn, a former member of the royalist group Thailand Help Centre for Cyberbullying Victims. Anon was later charged and indicted for royal defamation and violation of the Computer Crimes Act.
The Criminal Court on 17 January 2024 found Anon guilty and sentenced him to 4 years in prison. He subsequently filed an appeal.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) reported that the Appeal Court upheld the January 2024 verdict of the Criminal Court. It ruled that although he referred to the monarchy in most of his posts, one post mentioned the King. data.title: Inside Anon Nampa’s testimony on monarchy reform during royal defamation trial
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
Inside Anon Nampa’s testimony on monarchy reform during royal defamation trial
After five years of court hearings, the verdict in a royal defamation case arising from one of the largest protests on 19-20 September 2020 will be delivered on 16 December. Thai human rights lawyer Anon Nampa, the last defendant to testify, has maintained his innocence and defended his good intention to reform the monarchy.
The case stems from the 19-20 September 2020 protest at Sanam Luang and the nearby Thammasat University’s Tha Phra Chan campus. It was the second major protest held by the United Front of Thammasat and Demonstration (UFTD) and one of the biggest crowds in Thai contemporary history gathered at the campus.
The protest followed the UFTD’s first major and controversial protest on 10 August 2020 at Thammasat’s Rangsit Campus, where an activist read out the UFTD’s 10-point proposal calling for monarchy reform.
At that time, 22 pro-democracy activists were indicted in connection with the peaceful assembly, some of whom faced royal defamation charges, including Anon.
The hearings in this case took around five years, and the final hearing took place on 6 November, with Anon the last defendant to testify. The verdict will be delivered on 16 December.
Before the first hearing took place on 2 December 2021, the defendants faced difficulties obtaining and presenting important evidence for their defence, as the Court refused to subpoena documents which involved the monarchy, including records of the King’s personal expenses, and his travel itineraries to Germany during 2016-2020.
The role of monarchy in Thai politics through Anon’s eyes Anon has been a human rights lawyer since graduating. He has been a defence lawyer in royal defamation cases both before and after the 2020 mass protests.

data.title: No walk in the park for new Malaysian facilitator tackling Thailand’s southern insurgency
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
No walk in the park for new Malaysian facilitator tackling Thailand’s southern insurgency
Malaysia’s newly appointed facilitator for the peace talks between the Thai government and the Barisan Revolusi Nasional Melayu Patani (BRN) spent three days in Thailand this past week, introducing himself to a long list of officials.
Lt Gen (Rtd) Datuk Ahmad Norihan Jalal is no stranger to Thailand. A former head of intelligence at Malaysia’s Ministry of Defence, he has strong personal ties with many senior Thai military officers and knows well the staff of the Fourth Army Area, which oversees day-to-day security in the far South.
He is not the first Malaysian military man to hold the post. Gen Tan Sri Zulkifli Zainal Abidin, a retired chief of the Malaysian Armed Forces, became facilitator in January 2023. He replaced Tan Sri Abdul Rahim Noor, Malaysia’s fifth Inspector-General of Police and the man who gave Anwar Ibrahim, now Prime Minister, that infamous black eye.
In fact, Zulkifli’s name had been floated as early as the government of Prime Minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob, on the belief that a military man would deal better with the National Council for Peace and Order (NCPO), the grand title the Thai junta gave itself after the May 2014 coup.
Why Zulkifli was replaced after only 18 months remains unclear. He was not dropped altogether, however. He stayed on as Malaysia’s adviser and facilitator for the Mindanao peace process, which suggests a reassignment rather than a falling-out.
Zulkifli shared one view with Thai military leaders: neither wanted the mediation and facilitation crowded with international NGOs and foreign governments. What stalled the talks during his tenure was not the BRN but criticisms from the policy circle of the then-ruling Pheu Thai Party, where some felt the process was too lenient toward the rebels. data.title: 11 countries recommend amendments to royal defamation law during Thailand’s UPR process
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
11 countries recommend amendments to royal defamation law during Thailand’s UPR process
During Thailand’s Universal Periodic Review (UPR) session on 9 November, 11 countries raised concerns about the use of the royal defamation law to restrict freedom of expression.
Of these 11 countries, Germany, Mexico, Norway, Sweden, Austria and Demark recommended that Thailand review or amend the royal defamation law in line with international conventions like the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and other international human rights laws.
Finland recommended that the royal defamation law be amended so that there is no minimum sentence and that Thailand ensure the right to a fair trial and judicial independence. Sweden recommended the abolition of the mandatory minimum sentence for royal defamation, and called for children and minors to be exempted from criminal liability under the royal defamation law.
Ireland recommended amending or repealing laws that have been used to restrict freedoms of expression and peaceful assembly, including the royal defamation law. Canada, meanwhile, recommended amending or repealing the royal defamation law, the sedition law, and the Computer Crimes Act.
Some countries also recommended that Thailand ensure that the right to a fair trial is respected and end the prosecution of citizens exercising their right to freedom of expression, especially those who are minors. Some also recommended the amendment of other laws that have been used to restrict freedoms of expression and peaceful assembly, such as the sedition law and the Computer Crimes Act.
Thailand received a total of 276 recommendations from UN Member States. During the UPR adoption session on 13 November, Benjamin Sukanjanajtee, Permanent Representative of Thailand to the United Nations Office in Geneva, said that it is supporting 215 recommendations, while the remaining 61 will be given further consideration through consultation at the national level. data.title: Thailand urges Cambodia not to internationalise land border dispute
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
Thailand urges Cambodia not to internationalise land border dispute
Thailand has urged Cambodia not to internationalise the land border dispute, saying that it deeply regretted that Cambodia used the Francophonie and ASEAN summits to vilify Thailand. The remarks came amid an ongoing process to resolve the two countries’ maritime dispute through UN’s conciliation.
Speaking on 15 November at the Francophonie Summit’s opening in Phnom Penh, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet said that Thai troops still occupy parts of Cambodian territory after last year’s deadly border fighting, according to Camboja.
He said that about 20,000 Cambodians remain unable to return home, calling for existing agreements to be honoured and for joint border demarcation to resume. Hun Manet was also reported as saying that Cambodia did not initiate either of the two rounds of armed clashes with Thailand in 2025, adding that no borders had been altered through the use of armed force or the creation of faits accomplis.
In addition, the Cambodian representative at the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila delivered a similar message on the same day.
In response to the remark made by his Cambodian counterpart, PM Anutin Charnvirakul said that Thailand remained committed to resolving the differences peacefully through bilateral mechanisms and in accordance with international law.
He asserted that both Cambodia and Thailand must avoid internationalising all bilateral issues and should “advocate confidence-building measures with each other” if each side desires to restore friendship.
The Thai Foreign Ministry also issued an official statement expressing regret that Cambodia used its position as host of the meeting to highlight throughout the programme a number of unfounded allegations deliberately meant to vilify Thailand, particularly the claim that that Thailand occupies Cambodian territory and prevents approximately 20,000 Cambodian nationals from returning to their homes.

data.title: Bangkok’s EV Motorcycle Taxis Shoulder the Battery Burden
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Bangkok’s EV Motorcycle Taxis Shoulder the Battery Burden
When Samart Dornburan heads out to work as a motorcycle taxi driver, he takes four batteries with him. He uses three during the day and saves the fourth for the journey home. Each battery gives him a range of around 40–50 kilometres. If he runs out of power on the road, he has to pay someone to deliver a replacement.
“I’d earn 100 baht from fares, and 50 baht would go on paying someone to bring me a battery,” he recalled.
Samart has driven motorcycle taxis for more than 30 years and now heads the Bang Kruai Samakkhi motorcycle taxi stand in Nonthaburi province. He switched to an electric motorcycle during a pilot project that provided a shared battery-swapping station. But when the project ended, the station and spare batteries were taken away. He then began carrying his own batteries. Some fellow drivers sold their electric motorcycles, and Samart bought their vehicles and batteries to keep using them.

Meanwhile, the Thai–German Cooperation on Energy, Mobility and Climate project (TGC-EMC) estimates that Bangkok’s petrol-powered motorcycle taxis emit around 80,000–100,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide and approximately 16 tonnes of PM2.5 annually.

data.title: Myanmar migrant leader arrested over his birth record, denied bail
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Myanmar migrant leader arrested over his birth record, denied bail
Weera Saengthong, a leader of the Myanmar migrant network Bright Future who has been protesting Myanmar-run CI centers in Thailand, has been arrested and detained without bail over allegations that he used false evidence to obtain a Thai birth certificate.
Weera, also known as Suraj Giri, turned himself into the police in Kanchanaburi on 13 November. An arrest warrant was issued for him on 9 November after the Sai Yok District Registration Office revoked his birth certificate.
Registration officials said that five witnesses who supported his birth registration gave statements in 2010 that did not match, that checks found inconsistencies in his stated place of birth and date of entry, and that he did not produce further evidence within the 30 days he was given.
Democratic Voice of Burma (DVB) reported that Weera has been denied bail and remains in detention.
Local media reported that Songchai Niamhom, member of the ultra-royalist King Protection Group, filed a complaint with the Ministry of Interior claiming that Weera used false evidence to obtain a Thai birth certificate and an ID card known as the “Number 0 card” issued for unregistered individuals, stateless persons, or members of ethnic communities.
Weera was assaulted on 1 November by members of ultra-royalist groups during a protest staged by the Bright Future network calling for the abolition of Myanmar-run Certificate of Identity (CI) centres in Thailand and for the Thai-issued “pink card” to be accepted as workers’ only identity document as they see the CI centres as a way for the Myanmar regime to exploit workers.
At about 11.30am, members of two royalist groups confronted Weera: the People’s Centre for the Protection of the Monarchy, led by Anon Klinkaew, and the King Protection Group, led by Songchai Niamhom. data.title: Supreme Court sentences 29-year-old activist to prison over FB post
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Supreme Court sentences 29-year-old activist to prison over FB post
The Supreme Court today (19 November) sentenced activist Pimchanok Jirataiyanon, 29, to 2 years in prison on a royal defamation charge over a Facebook post made in 2022.
The post in question said “The government is shit, the institution is shit,” which a complainant interpreted as intended to refer to the royal institution without mentioning it explicitly.
The activist was apprehended at her residence in Bangkok on 18 March 2022, without having received a prior summons.
She testified that she did not refer to the royal institution as accused, but rather an educational institution. In addition, she argued that the royal defamation law covers only the King, the Queen, the Heir Apparent, and the Regent, rather than the whole royal institution.
In September 2023, the Chiang Mai Provincial Court found her guilty on the grounds that despite not mentioning any specific monarch, the royal defamation law protects the monarchy as an institution. She was sentenced to 3 years in prison, reduced to 2 years because she gave useful testimony. In April 2025, the Appeal Court upheld the ruling.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) said today (19 November) that the Supreme Court upheld the verdict, finding her guilty on the grounds that the royal defamation law exists not only to protect the reputation of the King, the Queen, the Heir Apparent, and the Regent, but also to protect national security and to protect the King as the head of state and one of the country’s main institutions. It noted that Pimchanok is an activist who has participated in “anti-monarchy” activities, as well as participated in protests demanding the repeal of the royal defamation law and the release of political prisoners, and so it believes the post refers to the monarchy.
Pimchanok is serving her sentence at the Chiang Mai Women Correctional Institution. Her detention brings the number of people detained on royal defamation charges to 35.
